name: Cyprian of Carthage

seo.title: St Cyprian of Carthage: plague, martyrdom, quotes and feast days
seo.description: Who Cyprian of Carthage was, in plain words: the plague, his martyrdom, his famous lines with the book and chapter, and his feast days East and West.

band.lede: Rich orator turned bishop of Carthage, who led his church through persecution and plague and died a martyr.

picture.alt: Saint Cyprian as a bishop in a gold mitre and green cloak, holding a sword and a martyr's palm, with his name painted on a panel below
picture.credit: Saint Cyprian, Master of Messkirch, about 1535-1540. Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. Public domain.
picture.creator: Master of Messkirch

card.line: Rich orator turned bishop of Carthage, who led his church through persecution and plague and died a martyr.

filters.alias: thascius caecilius cyprianus kyprianos cyprien hieromartyr carthage

who: Cyprian was a rich teacher of public speaking in Carthage. He became a Christian about 246, and the city's bishop two years later. He led his church through persecution, plague and quarrels, often by letter from hiding. He argued hard with the bishop of Rome. In 258 he was beheaded, the first bishop of Carthage to die a martyr.

roles.name: Convert
roles.line: Sold his estates for the poor

lines: About two years, when made bishop
About two in hiding or exile
Each gave his view in turn

numbers.src: Letter 59, to the bishops of Numidia

lines: He told his friends to pay them

facts.label: Born
facts.text: Probably about 200. No early source says where. It is usually given as **Carthage**, near today's **Tunis**, where he spent all his known life.

facts.label: Before he was a Christian
facts.text: A famous teacher of public speaking, a pleader in the courts, and a rich man. His deacon Pontius passes over these years on purpose.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **14 September 258**, beheaded with the sword on the estate of Sextus, near Carthage.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: By night, with tapers and torches, in the burial ground of Macrobius Candidianus on the Mappalian Way.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: His full name was **Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus**. The court called him Thascius Cyprianus. At his baptism he took the name Caecilius, from the priest who converted him. The Orthodox call him **Hieromartyr Cyprian**: a martyr who was a bishop.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint and martyr to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: As a bishop in a mitre, with a sword for how he died and a palm for a martyr. The Master of Messkirch painted him so, about 1535.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: About a dozen short books in Latin, and many letters. The best known is **On the Unity of the Church**.

portrait.alt: A Byzantine fresco of a grey-bearded bishop with a gold halo, in pale robes and a white stole marked with black crosses, holding an open scroll; Greek letters beside him read Saint Cyprian
portrait.credit: St Cyprian, fresco, Panagia tou Arakos, Lagoudera, Cyprus, late 12th century. Photo: Dumbarton Oaks, CC0.
portrait.caption: A fresco in a church at Lagoudera, Cyprus, from the late 12th century. The Greek beside him reads only Saint Cyprian. Greek churches long merged him with a legendary Cyprian of Antioch, so this may be the bishop of that merged story. Photo: Dumbarton Oaks, CC0.

west.text: **Episcopal Church**, in Lesser Feasts and Fasts.
The day he died. The **1916 Roman Martyrology** names him here, and keeps his feast on the 16th.
**Catholic** memorial, shared with Pope Cornelius. Also Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: **OCA**. Also the **Russian Church**, on the old calendar. That is 13 September on today's calendar.
Popular **Greek** calendars, which merge him with the legendary Cyprian of Antioch.

feasts.note: Jerome says he died on the same day of the year as Pope Cornelius, “but not in the same year”. The Catholic Church keeps the two together on the 16th. The 14th is also Holy Cross Day. The Church of England keeps Cyprian the day after it, and the Episcopal Church the day before.

traits.title: grave and warm at once
traits.text: His deacon says his face was serious and glad together. “Neither was his severity gloomy, nor his affability excessive.” People could not tell whether he deserved more to be revered or to be loved. Pontius settles it: “he deserved both to be revered and to be loved.”

traits.title: gave it away
traits.text: Early in his faith he sold whole estates and gave the money to the poor. As bishop he was asked about an actor who no longer performed but still taught acting. He must give it up, Cyprian said. If he was poor, the church would keep him, “if he be content, that is, with very frugal but innocent food.”

cite.text: Pontius, Life, chapter 2; Letter 60, to Euchratius

traits.title: forgave his opponents
traits.text: Some of the clergy opposed his election. Pontius says Cyprian forgave them and counted them among his closest friends, “to the astonishment of many”. Not all were won over. The Catholic Encyclopedia says five priests stayed his enemies.

traits.title: a sharp pen, an open door
traits.text: In a quarrel he did not soften his words. He wrote of “the bitter obstinacy of our brother Stephen”, the bishop of Rome. Yet he opened his great council by saying no bishop would be cut off for disagreeing. They would go on “judging no man, nor rejecting any one from the right of communion, if he should think differently from us.”

cite.text: Letter 73, to Pompey; The Seventh Council of Carthage

traits.title: changed his mind, and said so
traits.text: While the persecution raged, he was stern with those who had fallen. Afterwards he let the repentant back after penance. He owned the change openly. Both, he wrote, were done “not without long-balanced and pondered reasons.”

said.lede: His deacon Pontius shared his exile and wrote his Life soon after he died. Later writers praised his style, and argued with his views.

quotes.q: The blessed Cyprian like a fountain of pure water flows softly and sweetly
quotes.who: Jerome, about 395. He adds that Cyprian “has nowhere discussed the divine scriptures”.

quotes.q: …his error was compensated by his remaining in catholic unity, and by the abundance of his charity; and finally it was cleared away by the pruning-hook of martyrdom.
quotes.who: Augustine, who thought him wrong about baptism

cite.text: On Baptism, Against the Donatists, Book 1, chapter 18

quotes.q: Cyprianus, therefore, was above all others distinguished and renowned
quotes.who: Lactantius, about 305. He also tells how a clever critic mocked him “by the change of a single letter”, as Coprianus. The English editors explain it as a word for low jesters.

moments.title: A new man
moments.text: An old priest named Caecilius brought him to faith. Cyprian had not believed he could ever shed habits as deep as his. “I used to indulge my sins as if they were actually parts of me,” he wrote. After baptism, what had seemed impossible became possible.

cite.text: To Donatus, chapters 3 and 4; Pontius, Life, chapter 2

moments.title: Made bishop
moments.text: He was still new to the faith when the people wanted him as their bishop. He stepped back, “giving place to men of older standing”. But the people would not have it. “A crowded fraternity was besieging the doors of the house”, says Pontius. When he came, they greeted him with great joy.

moments.title: Leading by letter
moments.text: In January 250 the emperor Decius published an edict against Christians. In Carthage the crowds called again and again for Cyprian to be thrown to the lions. He went into hiding and led his church by letter. The clergy at Rome heard of it. Their letter reports that he “acted quite rightly”. Then it quotes Jesus on the hireling who “seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth”. Cyprian sent them thirteen of his letters, to show what he had done.

moments.title: Second chances
moments.text: Many in Carthage had given in. Several thousand had bought certificates saying they had sacrificed. When the storm passed, many wanted to come back. Cyprian chose a middle way: real penance, then return. He would be neither “too ungentle and pertinacious in repelling their repentance” nor “too lax and easy in rashly yielding communion”. At Carthage and at Rome, groups broke away from their bishops. At Rome, Novatian refused the fallen any way back and set himself up as a rival bishop. Cyprian wrote On the Unity of the Church against such splits.

moments.title: The plague
moments.text: A plague swept the city. People abandoned the sick, even their own. Cyprian called his church together. He told them there was “nothing wonderful in our cherishing our own people only”. They must help everyone, even those who persecuted them. Those too poor to give money gave their work. So good was done, says Pontius, “to all men, not to those only who are of the household of faith.”

moments.title: The quarrel with Rome
moments.text: Cyprian held that anyone baptised by heretics must be baptised again. Stephen, the bishop of Rome, said no: hands should only be laid on them. Eusebius says Stephen “was very indignant at this”. In September 256, 87 bishops met at Carthage under Cyprian and stood with him. Stephen would not even receive their messengers. Neither side gave way. After that, says the Catholic Encyclopedia, “we know no more of the controversy.”

cite.text: Eusebius, Church History, Book 7, chapter 3; Letter 74, from Firmilian; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: Exile
moments.text: The emperor Valerian renewed the persecution. On 30 August 257 the proconsul questioned Cyprian at Carthage. He answered, “I am a Christian and a bishop.” He was sent into exile at Curubis. His deacon Pontius went with him.

cite.text: Acts of Cyprian, chapter 1; Pontius, Life, chapter 12

extras.title: Visions and wonders
extras.lede: Pontius tells of no miracles worked by Cyprian. What the early sources record are visions, and wonders at the Eucharist. Cyprian says he saw one of them himself.

items.title: His death foretold
items.text: On his first night in exile, as he was falling asleep, he saw a very tall young man. The young man led him before the proconsul, who wrote a sentence on his tablet. The young man did not say it aloud. He showed it with his hand. Cyprian begged for one day's delay, and the young man signed that it was granted. Cyprian told this himself, and Pontius gives it in his words. Pontius says the day stood for a year. Cyprian died a year later, on the very day of the vision.
items.quote: with hand expanded and flattened like a blade, he imitated the stroke of the accustomed punishment

items.title: The persecution foreseen
items.text: He wrote to his clergy of a vision. A father of a family sat with a sad young man at his right hand. At his left stood one with a net, glad of the chance to destroy. Cyprian does not say who saw it. He says it was shown before the persecution came, and came true.
items.quote: This was shown long before the tempest of this devastation arose. And we have seen that which had been shown fulfilled

items.title: The child and the cup
items.text: “Learn what occurred when I myself was present and a witness.” A baby girl had been fed bread and wine left from a pagan sacrifice, while her parents fled. Her mother, not knowing, brought her to church. The child wept, turned her face away and shut her mouth against the cup. The deacon made her take a little. Then she sobbed and was sick.
items.quote: In a profane body and mouth the Eucharist could not remain

items.title: Fire and a cinder
items.text: A woman kept the Eucharist in a box. She “tried with unworthy hands to open her box”, and fire rose from it. A man who had fallen took his share in secret, and found only a cinder in his hands. Cyprian reports these two, but does not say he saw them.
items.quote: was deterred by fire rising from it from daring to touch it

items.title: Doubted by his English editor
items.text: The editor of the English translation did not believe these stories. He wrote that many things were “sincerely believed and honestly recorded” that a careful reader will not accept. He quoted the historian Henry Milman: “In what a high-wrought state of enthusiasm must men have been, who could relate and believe such statements as miraculous!” The American editor answered in a note that believers should not be charged with “exceptional credulity”.
items.quote: many circumstances were sincerely believed and honestly recorded, which will not be for a moment received as true by the calm and critical reader

cite.text: Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 5, introduction to Cyprian

extras.title: His hardest words
extras.lede: Some of what he wrote is hard to read today. Here it is in his own words, beside what others have said.

items.title: The Jews
items.text: He gathered Bible passages under headings, in a handbook for a man named Quirinus. The English edition calls it Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews. His preface says the first book shows that the Jews “had departed from God, and had lost God's favour”, while the Christians took their place. The Catholic Encyclopedia describes it as passages arranged “to illustrate the passing away of the Old Law and its fulfillment in Christ”.
items.quote: That the Jews have fallen under the heavy wrath of God, because they have departed from the Lord, and have followed idols.

cite.text: Testimonies, preface and Book 1, the first heading

items.title: No salvation outside the Church
items.text: He held that no one outside the Church can be saved. Not even dying for Christ helps a heretic, he wrote, “because there is no salvation out of the Church”. He says the same in On the Unity of the Church. His own Latin is usually given as {la|salus extra ecclesiam non est}. The neater {la|Extra ecclesiam nulla salus} is often called his, but it is not his wording.
items.quote: He cannot be a martyr who is not in the Church

cite.text: Letter 72, to Jubaianus; On the Unity of the Church, chapter 14

items.title: He lost the argument on baptism
items.text: The Western Church came to side with Stephen. Augustine called him “that holy man”, but said he held “an opinion at variance with the true view”. Jerome claims the African bishops later dropped the practice themselves. The American editor of his letters, an Episcopal bishop, drew a sharper point.
items.quote: on the Roman theory, this glorious martyr died in schism. He is, nevertheless, a canonized saint in the Roman Calendar.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia; Augustine, On Baptism, Book 1, chapter 18; Jerome, Against the Luciferians; Ante-Nicene Fathers, note to Letter 82

items.title: Women's make-up
items.text: He wrote that not only virgins and widows but all women should leave their faces as God made them. No hair dye, no eye black, no rouge.
items.quote: the work of God and His fashioning and formation ought in no manner to be adulterated, either with the application of yellow colour, or with black dust or rouge

cite.text: On the Dress of Virgins, chapter 15

words.note: He wrote in Latin. These lines are from R. E. Wallis's translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers (1886).

feature.kicker: To a church split in two, 251
feature.q: He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother.
feature.ctx: Against those who broke away from their bishops. In Latin, {la|Habere jam non potest Deum patrem, qui Ecclesiam non habet matrem.}

cite.text: On the Unity of the Church, chapter 6

quotes.q: All our power is of God; I say, of God.
quotes.who: On his own conversion, soon after his baptism.

quotes.q: For custom without truth is the antiquity of error.
quotes.who: Against Rome's appeal to custom, in the quarrel over baptism.

quotes.q: For God is the hearer, not of the voice, but of the heart.
Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one, but for the whole people, because we the whole people are one.
quotes.who: On praying for everyone, not for ourselves alone.

quotes.q: They think that they possess, when they are rather possessed
quotes.who: On the rich who denied Christ to keep their property.

quotes.q: We regard paradise as our country—we already begin to consider the patriarchs as our parents: why do we not hasten and run, that we may behold our country, that we may greet our parents?
quotes.who: To a church dying of plague.

myths.claim: He was a magician, converted by the virgin Justina. The Prayer of St Cyprian against witchcraft is his.
myths.truth: That is Cyprian of Antioch, a figure of legend. Gregory of Nazianzus and the poet Prudentius already mixed the two men up, says the Catholic Encyclopedia, “a mistake often repeated”. It adds: “It is certain that no Bishop of Antioch bore the name of Cyprian.” Popular Greek calendars still merge the two on 2 October.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, Sts. Cyprian and Justina; saint.gr

myths.claim: He taught that the whole Church rests on the pope, as the heir of Peter.
myths.truth: Chapter 4 of On the Unity of the Church comes down in two forms. One adds that “the primacy is given to Peter”. The notes to the English translation call such lines “beyond all question spurious”. The Catholic Encyclopedia says it is “now generally admitted” that Cyprian made the change himself. It also says that by one chair he always meant the bishop's chair. Both sides agree he held that all the apostles had equal power.

cite.text: On the Unity of the Church, chapter 4, with the editors' notes; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: He ran from persecution to save his own skin.
myths.truth: He did hide in 250. He said he left so that his presence would not stir up the crowds further. In 258 friends begged him to escape, and offered him places to go. He refused. He hid only once more, so that he would not be tried at Utica. He wanted to die before his own people, “that I may confess among you, and there suffer, and thence depart to the Lord even as I ought.”

cite.text: Letter 14; Pontius, Life, chapter 14; Letter 82, his last

myths.truth: He was beheaded with the sword. The mistake goes back to Theodoret, who wrote that he “found a death in the fire”. An editor of Theodoret notes that this “is either an error, or means the fiery trial of martyrdom”.

cite.text: Theodoret, Letter 151, with the editor's note; Acts of Cyprian

myths.claim: He nursed the plague victims and buried the dead with his own hands.
myths.truth: The OCA's life says he “tended the sick and buried the dead himself”. Pontius, who was there, says Cyprian rallied his people to care for everyone, and they did the work. The Catholic Encyclopedia says he “raised a staff of workers and a great fund of money”.

cite.text: Pontius, Life, chapters 9 and 10; OCA; Catholic Encyclopedia

stood.lede: Each line is his own, in R. E. Wallis's translation. Letters are numbered as in the Ante-Nicene Fathers.

circle.name: Caecilius
circle.text: An old priest of Carthage who brought him to faith. Cyprian took his name. When Caecilius was dying, he left his wife and children in Cyprian's care.

cite.text: Pontius, Life, chapter 4; Jerome, Illustrious Men, chapter 67

circle.name: Pontius
circle.text: His deacon. He went into exile with him and wrote his Life. Jerome calls it “a notable volume”.

circle.name: Tertullian
circle.text: His master, in books. An old man who had been Cyprian's secretary told Jerome that Cyprian read Tertullian every day. He would often say, “Give me the master”, meaning Tertullian.

circle.name: Cornelius of Rome
circle.text: Bishop of Rome when Novatian split from him. Cyprian backed Cornelius and wrote to him often. Jerome says they died on the same day of the year. They share a feast.

cite.text: Jerome, Illustrious Men, chapter 67; The Roman Martyrology (1916)

circle.name: Novatian
circle.text: A Roman priest who refused any way back to those who had lapsed. He set himself up as a rival bishop of Rome. Cyprian treated him as a schismatic.

circle.name: Stephen of Rome
circle.text: Bishop of Rome, who would not have people baptised by heretics baptised again. Cyprian wrote of his “bitter obstinacy”.

circle.name: Firmilian of Caesarea
circle.text: A bishop in Cappadocia who took Cyprian's side. He wrote of “this so open and manifest folly of Stephen”.

circle.name: Florentius Puppianus
circle.text: A confessor of the persecution who doubted Cyprian was a true bishop. Cyprian's answer asks, “what swelling of pride is this, what arrogance of soul, what inflation of mind”.

circle.name: Xistus of Rome
circle.text: Stephen's successor, also called Sixtus. Pontius calls him “the good and peace-making priest”. A few weeks before his own death, Cyprian heard that Xistus had been killed in a cemetery at Rome on 6 August 258.

death.big: He was beheaded on 14 September 258, on an estate near Carthage.
paras: Called back from exile, he waited at Carthage. On 13 September two officials came for him. He was held overnight in an officer's house. His people kept watch in the street outside.

In the morning the proconsul, Galerius Maximus, told him the emperors commanded him to perform the rite. He said, “I refuse.” Told to think of his own good, he answered, “Do as you are bid. In so clear a case there is no need for consideration.” The proconsul gave sentence “hardly and reluctantly”: death by the sword. The crowd cried, “Let us also be beheaded with him.”

He was led out to the estate of Sextus. People climbed into the trees to see. He took off his cloak, knelt and prayed. He told his friends to give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces. He bound his own eyes, and two clergy, both named Julianus, tied the ends for him.
The executioner's hand shook so that he could hardly grip the sword. Then, says Pontius, the centurion was strengthened “with power granted from above”.

later.title: Later reports
later.text: The Acts say his body was laid out nearby for the pagans to see. By night it was carried with tapers and torches to the burial ground of Macrobius Candidianus. The 1916 Roman Martyrology adds that his bones were later carried from Africa to Lyons, in France.

cite.text: Acts of Cyprian, chapter 5; The Roman Martyrology (1916), 17 July

items.k: To an officer who offered him dry clothes
items.q: We apply medicines to annoyances which probably to-day will no longer exist.

cite.text: Pontius, Life, chapter 16; Acts of Cyprian, chapter 4

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint and martyr. Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: A memorial on 16 September, with Cornelius
A hieromartyr. 31 August in the OCA
A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: He was honoured from the first. The court record of his death ends by calling him “the most blessed martyr Cyprian”.

His name is also said in the Roman Canon, the old Eucharistic Prayer of the Latin Mass. Its first list of saints names twelve martyrs. The Catholic Encyclopedia says all the others are local saints of Rome.

Popular Greek calendars give him no day of his own. They fold him into the legend of Cyprian of Antioch, on 2 October. The Greek New Synaxaristis of Hieromonk Makarios of Simonopetra (2001) does give him a life of his own, in its September volume.

quotes.q: …St. Cyprian (d. 258), who had a serious misunderstanding with a Roman pope, is the only foreigner honoured by the Roman Church by being named among her own martyrs.
quotes.who: The Catholic Encyclopedia, 1908, on the Roman Canon

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, Canon of the Mass
